verses.translation_literal: And YHWH said to Abram, Go-you, for-yourself, from your land and from your kindred and from the house of your father, to the land which I will show you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the LORD spoke to Abram, and the word was an order and a door at once: Go. Go from your land, from the people who bore you, from the house of your father. Go to a land that I will show you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a command with no map attached. Three leavings are named in a tightening spiral: land, then kindred or birthplace, then the father's house, which is the innermost circle of an ancient person's security, since land, protection and inheritance all ran through the household. Radak and Ramban both read the order as deliberately painful, each step costlier than the last, and the destination is withheld on purpose: Radak notes that a promised land as good as the old one would have been easy, but "the land which I will show you" gives Abram nothing to weigh (Radak on Genesis 12:1).

The opening two words are one imperative and a dative of the same sound: lekh ("go") and lekha ("for yourself"). They are not two verbs and not a doubled "go". The sound is a deliberate rhyme, and the second word is the ethical dative, a very common Hebrew idiom for "on your own behalf", as in "he went off" (Exod 18:27) or "I will go" (Jer 5:5), which Radak and Ramban cite to show it is ordinary usage. Rashi reads it as "for your benefit and your good" (Rashi on Genesis 12:1); Ramban says no such special meaning is needed. Actors can use either: a blessing hidden in a command, or a plain "off you go".

KJV audit: "Now the Lord had said" imposes a pluperfect; the Hebrew is a plain narrative "and YHWH said", and the question of whether this word came in Ur or in Haran is argued by Ibn Ezra, Radak and Ramban from the text, not settled by the verb form. "Get thee out" is archaic and brusque where the Hebrew is a bare "go", and "country" and "a land" lose the article: the Hebrew has ha'aretz, "the land", though it names no place. The ending "I will show you" uses the verb r-ʼ-h, "to see", which returns in verse 7 when the LORD himself appears.

philological_notes.note: One imperative (lekh, 'go') followed by a dative of the same sound (lekha, 'for yourself'). The ethical dative is common with verbs of motion; Radak and Ramban give parallels. Rashi reads it as 'for your benefit and good'; Ramban rejects the need for that.
'Your kindred' or 'place of your birth': from y-l-d, 'to bear'. Ramban takes it as both birthplace and the family born there.
'I will show you', a causative (hiphil) of r-ʼ-h, 'to see'. The same root appears as the passive 'he appeared' (vayyera) in verse 7.

verses.translation_literal: And I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will make great your name, and be a blessing.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will make of you a nation, a great one. I will bless you. I will make your name great. And you yourself, Abram, will be a blessing.
verses.directors_commentary:
Four promises answer the three losses of verse 1: a nation for the lost land, a blessing for the lost kin, a great name for the lost father's house. Rashi says the road itself shrinks three things, children, wealth and reputation, so each is promised back. All this to a childless man of seventy-five whose wife is barren (Radak): the actor should play that irony, not the grandeur.

The KJV's 'shalt be a blessing' turns the last verb into a prediction. The Hebrew is an imperative, vehyeh: 'be a blessing', so that the promise ends with a command. Radak reads it as an imperative standing in for the future; Rashi hears a transfer of authority: until now God blessed, from now on you do. The word 'great' is also repeated: a great nation, a name made great. In Genesis 11 the builders of Babel wanted to 'make a name' for themselves; here a name is received, not seized.

philological_notes.note: An imperative, 'and be', not a future. Radak takes it as an imperative used in place of a future (compare Deut 32:50); Rashi hears a handing-over of the power to bless.
The piel 'I will make great' echoes the 'great' of 'great nation'; the repeated root ties nation and name together.

verses.translation_literal: And I will bless those who bless you, and the one who belittles you I will curse, and in you will be blessed all the clans of the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: Those who bless you, I will bless. The one who holds you light, I will curse. And through you, Abram, every clan on the face of the earth will find itself blessed.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the hinge of the speech: the promise turns from Abram to everyone else. Ibn Ezra points to a small asymmetry the English hides: the blessers are plural, 'those who bless', but the one who curses is singular. Radak adds that cursers will be few. God is promising a crowd of friends and a lone enemy.

There are two different Hebrew verbs here that the KJV renders with one word. The first, qalal, in 'meqallelkha', is 'to treat as light, to belittle'; the second, 'arar, is the heavy curse that binds. The line says: whoever treats you lightly, I will bind. The KJV's 'curseth' flattens that into a mirror image. The last clause is the most debated in Genesis: nivrekhu is a Niphal, which can be passive, 'will be blessed in you', or reflexive, 'will bless themselves by you', meaning people will say 'may you be like Abraham' (Rashi, Ramban). Rashbam in the packet reads a third sense: families will be mingled into yours. The KJV, 'in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed', picks the passive and also uses 'earth' for adamah, which is literally the ground, the soil of Genesis 2-3: the same ground that was cursed is to be blessed through him.

philological_notes.note: 'One who belittles you', literally treats as light (qll). Different root from the 'arar' of the response. Ibn Ezra notes the singular against the plural 'those who bless'.
Niphal, passive 'be blessed' or reflexive 'bless themselves'. Rashi reads it as people saying 'be like Abraham'; Rashbam reads a sense of mixing into your family.
'The ground', not the general word for earth, 'eretz'. It recalls the cursed ground of Genesis 3 and 'the clans of the ground' of Genesis 10.

token_glosses.gloss: and the one who belittles you

verses.translation_literal: And Abram went as YHWH had spoken to him, and Lot went with him; and Abram was a son of five years and seventy years when he went out from Haran.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abram went, just as the LORD had spoken to him. Lot went with him. Abram was seventy-five years old on the day he walked out of Haran.
verses.directors_commentary:
The obedience is told in one flat verb: he went. There is no speech, no hesitation and no question, which Radak reads as trust that needed no testing. The verb 'went' is the same lekh as the command of verse 1, so the sentence echoes the order: the first thing Abram does is obey exactly the word he was given.

The KJV, ASV and Webster say 'departed'; the Hebrew uses the plain verb 'went' twice, once for Abram and once for Lot, and the plainness is the point. Note that Lot 'went with him' is added as a second, separate verb: Lot is a follower, not a party to the call. Seventy-five is a flat number in Hebrew idiom, 'a son of five years and seventy years', which is how ages were stated in the ancient Near East; a man of that age was long past the usual age for starting a migration, and the packet's Radak notes he left his father behind.

philological_notes.note: 'Just as he had spoken': obedience measured against the exact word. Radak: Abram did not ask for proof, he believed.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram took Sarai his wife and Lot the son of his brother and all their property which they had gathered and the persons whom they had made in Haran, and they went out to go to the land of Canaan, and they came to the land of Canaan.
verses.translation_dramatic: Abram took Sarai, his wife, and Lot, his brother's son. He took all they had gathered, every flock and store, and all the people they had won in Haran. They went out, bound for the land of Canaan. And to the land of Canaan they came.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a caravan inventory: wife, nephew, goods, and a household of dependents. The words 'ha-nefesh asher asu', literally 'the persons they had made', do not mean 'souls' as the KJV and ASV have it, which sounds like conversions to a modern ear. The packet's commentators disagree: Rashi and the targums read it as people Abram and Sarai brought to the faith, 'made' as in raised or formed; Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as slaves and servants acquired, parallel to Deuteronomy 8:17 ('made me this wealth'). The Hebrew uses nefesh, 'person', in the singular as a collective. Under either reading, a company of dozens or hundreds is moving, with livestock: this is a migrating clan, not a lone prophet.

The verse ends with a deliberate doubling, 'to go to the land of Canaan, and to the land of Canaan they came', where the second clause finishes what Terah's family had begun and abandoned at Haran (Sforno, citing Genesis 11:31). The KJV's 'substance' is a good Early Modern word for property, but the Hebrew rekhush is movable goods, mainly livestock.

philological_notes.note: 'The persons they had made.' Rashi: converts, or slaves bought; Radak and Ibn Ezra: servants acquired, as in 'made me this wealth' (Deut 8:17); Onkelos: 'subjected to the Torah'.
Movable property, chiefly herds (Ibn Ezra cites Genesis 13:6).

verses.translation_literal: And Abram passed through in the land as far as the place of Shechem, as far as the oak of Moreh; and the Canaanite [was] then in the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: Abram walked on through the land, mile after mile, as far as the place called Shechem, as far as the oak of Moreh. And the Canaanite was in the land then.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a walking verse, and the actors must carry the length of it: "passed through" is a long traverse, not an arrival, and the doubled "as far as" (ʼad ... ʼad) marks two stops on the same road, Shechem and then its oak. Sforno reads it as Abram refusing to settle anywhere until the LORD appeared as promised (Sforno on Genesis 12:6). The last clause is the flat, ominous note: "the Canaanite was then in the land". Play it unemphasized, as a fact on the horizon.

The tree has its own question. Elon is a tree word (oak or terebinth), which Ibn Ezra compares to elah, a kind of tree, though he allows it may mean a field. Onkelos translates "plain" (meshar), and Radak follows that; the KJV and Webster inherit this and print "the plain of Moreh", whereas the ASV and YLT say "oak". Moreh is read as a man's name by Ramban and Radak, and its root y-r-h means "to teach, to point". That connection to "teacher" is my own observation and no commentator in the packet makes it.

Rashi reads "the oak of Moreh" as Shechem itself: God showed Abram Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, where Israel later took the oath of the Torah (Rashi on Genesis 12:6). Radak gives the same two sites and cites Deuteronomy 11:30, "beside the oaks of Moreh", where Moses places them (Radak on Genesis 12:6). On "then in the land": Rashi reads it as the Canaanites progressively conquering the land from Shem's descendants, so the promise returns it to Abraham's seed (Rashi on Genesis 12:6); Radak adds that Abram's large herds grazed freely while those who held the pastures said nothing to him, which he calls a miracle (Radak on Genesis 12:6). The KJV's "Sichem" is an older spelling, and "passed through" is accurate.

philological_notes.note: A large tree, oak or terebinth. Ibn Ezra relates it to elah, a kind of tree, but allows the sense 'field'; Onkelos and Radak read 'plain' (meshar). The KJV 'plain' follows that tradition; the Hebrew word itself is a tree word.

Moreh: Ramban and Radak take it as a man's name, after whom the place is called; Ibn Ezra raises Mamre and a place-name. The root y-r-h means 'to teach' or 'to point'; any link to the sense here is my own reading.

'And the Canaanite was then in the land': a circumstantial clause. Rashi and Radak read 'then' as marking that the land was not yet Abraham's seed's; Ibn Ezra says there is a hidden matter ('let the wise be silent').

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH appeared to Abram and said, To your seed I will give this land. And he built there an altar to YHWH, the one who appeared to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then the LORD appeared to Abram, and spoke: To your children I will give this land. And Abram built an altar there, for the LORD who had let himself be seen.
verses.directors_commentary:
The long walk pays off in two beats: the LORD is seen, and the LORD speaks. The promise is stated with the object first: "to your seed I will give this land". Radak has God explain the order: Abram himself, a single man, cannot hold the land; he may move freely through it with his herds now, but the land will be given to his descendants when they are many (Radak on Genesis 12:7). Play the pause before Abram answers, because the answer is not words: he builds.

The verb "appeared" (vayyera) is the passive form of the verb "to see" in verse 1, where God said "the land which I will show you" (ʼarʼekha). The echo is my own observation from the shared root; Sforno ties the two together, reading Abram's refusal to pitch his tent until the LORD appeared as the fulfilment of "which I will show you" (Sforno on Genesis 12:1). The closing phrase "to YHWH, the one who appeared to him" stresses the same word again. Ramban takes it as thanks for the appearance itself, since until now no vision had come to Abram (Ramban on Genesis 12:7). Rashi says the altar is for the news of offspring and of the land (Rashi on Genesis 12:7). Radak reads it as an altar of thanksgiving (Radak on Genesis 12:7).

KJV audit: "Unto thy seed will I give this land" matches the Hebrew word order and the future sense ("I will give"), so there is nothing to correct. "Seed" is a literal rendering of zeraʼ, a collective singular; "offspring" in the literal layer would be equally accurate, and I kept "seed" in the literal layer to show the word.

philological_notes.note: 'He appeared' (literally 'was seen'), the niphal of r-ʼ-h. Ibn Ezra explains the form and takes it as prophetic vision. It answers the 'I will show you' (ʼarʼekha) of verse 1, a link that is my own observation; Sforno connects the two moments.
'To your seed': a collective singular, with the prepositional phrase placed first for emphasis. Radak reads it as the descendants who will inherit, not Abram himself.
'The one who appeared to him': a niphal participle used as a title for the LORD. Ibn Ezra takes it as a participle of the same form as the verb. Ramban reads the altar as thanks for the appearance.

verses.translation_literal: And he moved on from there to the hill-country east of Bethel, and pitched his tent, Bethel on the west and Ai on the east; and he built there an altar to YHWH, and called on the name of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: From there he broke camp and climbed toward the hills, east of Bethel, and pitched his tent. Bethel lay behind him to the west, Ai in front of him to the east. There he built another altar to the LORD, and he called out the name of the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram's tent is a flag: he pitches it on a hill between two towns, Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. Sforno says that this is deliberate: he stands between two sizeable settlements so that those who come will hear him. The directions are given in Hebrew by the sun: 'miyam' is literally 'from the sea', the Mediterranean to the west, and 'qedem' 'from the east', literally 'the front', since the Hebrew speaker faces the sunrise.

The KJV's 'called upon the name of the Lord' keeps a phrase that English readers hear as private prayer. The Hebrew vayiqra beshem YHWH is a public act: Ramban argues it means that Abram proclaimed the name aloud before the altar, teaching strangers, as Onkelos's 'prayed' is only part of it. Radak adds that he showed the local people why they should serve one God. The altar is the second one in a land where the Canaanites are 'then in the land': it makes a claim on the land in sound.

philological_notes.note: Written with a final he, read with a vav ('his tent'). Rashi, citing Genesis Rabbah, takes the written he as 'her tent': Abram pitched Sarai's tent first. Radak says he and vav alternate.
'He called on / in the name of YHWH': a public proclamation, not just prayer. Onkelos renders 'prayed'; Ramban argues for a loud proclamation to people, citing Genesis 26:25.

verses.translation_literal: And Abram journeyed, going and journeying toward the Negeb.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Abram struck camp again, and moved on, and moved on, step by step, south toward the dry country, the Negeb.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew stretches the walk with a double infinitive, 'haloch venasoa', literally 'going and pulling up stakes': a herdsman's progress, camp by camp, never settling. Rashi and Radak read it as stage after stage, each pitched for a month or more, and Sforno as the pattern of shepherds seeking pasture.

The KJV's 'going on still toward the south' is close in meaning, but the 'south' is a proper name too: Negeb comes from a word meaning 'dry', which is why it also means south for the Hebrew speaker, who thinks facing east. The Negeb is the semi-arid steppe south of Hebron where flocks can graze in winter rains only; to go there is to move toward thinner land, and the next verse's famine arrives on that road.

philological_notes.note: Two absolute infinitives: 'going and pulling up (tent stakes)', a journey in many stages. Radak: from place to place.
'Toward the Negeb'; Ibn Ezra links the name to Aramaic 'dry' (nagiv), the dry south.

verses.translation_literal: And there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was heavy in the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then famine came upon the land, and the famine lay heavy on it. And Abram went down to Egypt, to live there for a while as a stranger.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first test after the promise is hunger. Radak says it is one of the trials of Abram: yesterday he was told all families would be blessed through him, and today he must leave the land itself. Egypt is the obvious refuge. Its crops depend on the Nile and not on rain (Radak cites Deut 11:10), so even in a drought year in Canaan Egypt had grain, and a herding household with many dependents could not wait out a bad year.

The KJV's 'grievous' is a fine archaism for kaved, which is 'heavy': the same word is used of a heavy burden. The famine is literally weighing on the land. 'Went down' is geographical and literal: the road to Egypt runs downhill from the Judean hills. The infinitive 'lagur', 'to sojourn', is the verb of the resident alien, the ger, one who lives under another's protection without rights of his own. Radak and Sforno both stress that it means a temporary stay, not settling. Ramban does not spare Abram: he calls the descent a sin, as the one who left the land commanded. Tradition is divided, and the text itself passes no verdict.

philological_notes.note: 'To sojourn': to live as a protected foreigner, not as a citizen. Radak and Sforno: a temporary stay, not a settling.
'Heavy': the famine presses on the land like a weight; the KJV's 'grievous' keeps the sense of burden.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, as he drew near to enter Egypt, that he said to Sarai his wife, Behold now, I know that you are a woman beautiful of appearance.
verses.translation_dramatic: And as they drew near the border of Egypt, Abram turned to Sarai, his wife, and said quietly: Look, I know. I have always known what you are: a woman beautiful to look upon.
verses.directors_commentary:
The moment is the border. Abram has just travelled the whole way and says nothing until the Nile country is in sight, and then begins with a soft, almost courtly 'hinneh na', 'behold now' or 'please look', the language of a man about to ask for something. The commentators differ on why now: Rashi has a midrash that modesty had kept him from noticing until now, or that her beauty survived the road, and the plain sense that now it matters; Ramban says na does not mean 'now' but just points to a standing fact ('I have always known', as in Genesis 19:8) and that the danger lies in the royal city, where beautiful women were taken for the king and husbands killed. Radak agrees that na is only a manner of speech. Ibn Ezra adds that looks vary with climate.

The KJV's 'fair woman to look upon' is nice but keeps a Victorian glow; the Hebrew is exact: 'a woman beautiful of appearance', yefat mar'eh, a stock phrase for striking looks. The dramatic point is that the husband is about to turn the most intimate fact about his wife into a problem to be managed. This is Egypt as seen by a nomad from the hills: a place of kings, courts and appetites, as Sforno hears it.

philological_notes.note: 'Behold now / please': na is a particle of polite urgency, not necessarily a time word. Radak and Ramban say the knowledge is old, and the particle only marks the moment of speaking.
'Beautiful of appearance', a construct phrase.

verses.translation_literal: And it will be, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, This is his wife; and they will kill me, and you they will let live.
verses.translation_dramatic: It will happen. The Egyptians will see you, and they will say, This one is his wife. Then they will kill me. And you, they will keep alive.
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram's logic is a chain of futures, each joined by 'and they will': they will see, they will say, they will kill, they will let live. He is not afraid of being robbed of Sarai; he is afraid of being in the way. Radak's analysis is sharp: seizure of a wife would be a crime, but if the husband were killed once, the woman would be unclaimed and available. Ramban notes that in a royal city the custom was to bring the beautiful woman to the king and to find some pretext to kill her husband.

The last two words are the sting. The verb 'yechayyu', piel of 'to live', means 'let live' or 'keep alive': the same verb is used of sparing the women captured in war (Num 31:15, cited by Radak). The KJV's 'save thee alive' is Elizabethan for the same thing, but it sounds like a rescue; in Hebrew it is the verdict of those who spare a woman for their own use. The word order puts the killing first and 'you' first in the second half: 'me they will kill, and you they will keep'. Radak adds a theological note: Abram was right not to rely on a miracle, citing the principle that one should not depend on divine intervention in danger.

philological_notes.note: Piel, 'they will let live / keep alive', as with captive women in war (Num 31:15). Radak: they will spare you for their pleasure.
'This is his wife': the Egyptians' imagined words, a bare identification which is a death sentence for Abram.

verses.translation_literal: Say, please: my sister [are] you, so that it may go well for me on your account, and my soul will live for your sake.
verses.translation_dramatic: Say it. Only say it: you are my sister. Then it will go well with me because of you, and I will go on living, for your sake.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a man bargaining for his life with the only currency he thinks he has. Abram is a landless immigrant, a resident alien with no clan around him, and in the ancient Near East such a man had no protection: a foreign husband stood in the way of a king's desire, and a foreign brother did not. Notice the Hebrew leans on one repeated idea in two forms: ba'avurekh and biglalekh both mean 'on your account', so the whole plea is built from 'because of you' twice over, and the second half names the stake plainly: nafshi, 'my soul', 'my life'. Sarai is asked to make the lie, and Abram lets her carry the danger.

The KJV's 'I pray thee' turns the small particle na into archaic courtesy; it is closer to 'please, I beg you'. Its 'thou art my sister' is fine, but 'soul' for nefesh is easy to misread as something spiritual: here it is breath and life itself. Watch the verb yitav, 'it may go well': it comes back, in the causative, in verse 16, where the thing Abram asked for arrives and the bitter irony begins. Ibn Ezra already draws that line, glossing 'it will go well for me' as a gift, and pointing to 12:16.

philological_notes.note: 'May it go well'. The same root returns as heitiv in v. 16, 'he did good to Abram'. Abram's wish is granted, at Sarai's expense. Ibn Ezra reads the phrase as a gift (dorón u-minchah) and points to 12:16.
'My soul' means my life, my self, the breath that can be stopped. The sense here is physical survival.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, as Abram entered Egypt-ward, and the Egyptians saw the woman, that beautiful [was] she, very.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so it happened. Abram came down into Egypt, and the Egyptians looked at the woman, and saw how beautiful she was. Exceedingly beautiful.
verses.directors_commentary:
Abram's fear is proved right in a single glance. The narrator does not say 'Sarai' here, only 'the woman': she is seen as an object before she is named as a person, and the Egyptians are the ones doing the seeing. The verb is the same one used all through Genesis for desire that begins in the eyes (compare Eve's tree, 3:6). The Hebrew ends on a flat, heavy word: me'od, 'very', stranded at the end of the verse.

The ending -ah on mitzrayemah is the directional suffix, 'Egypt-ward', and the KJV's 'into Egypt' loses the motion of a journey with a destination. 'Fair' in the KJV has aged: yafah is simply 'beautiful', and 'beheld' dresses a plain 'saw'. Rashi reads the clumsy phrasing 'as Abram entered' as a hint that he hid her in a chest and that the customs officials, demanding duty, opened it and saw her; that is his own reading from the phrase, not something the text says.

philological_notes.note: Egypt with the directional ending -ah: 'to Egypt', 'Egypt-ward'. The verse keeps the movement of the arrival.
'Beautiful'. KJV 'fair' is archaic. The following me'od 'very' is placed last for emphasis.

verses.translation_literal: And they saw her, the officials of Pharaoh, and they praised her to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken [to] the house of Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pharaoh's officials saw her too. They sang her praises to Pharaoh, and the woman was taken. Taken into Pharaoh's house.
verses.directors_commentary:
Beauty travels up the chain of command. First the common Egyptians, then the sarim, the king's officials, whose job was to bring the court what pleased it, and who praise her to Pharaoh in the manner of courtiers presenting a gift. The verb vayehallu comes from hll, 'to praise', the root of 'hallelujah'; the KJV's 'commended her' is a courteous word for what is really a sales pitch. 'Pharaoh', pharaoh in Egyptian per-aa, means 'great house', so the last words of the verse, 'the house of Pharaoh', say 'the great house of the Great House'.

The decisive verb is passive: vatukkach, 'she was taken'. No one is named as the one who takes. Radak, citing the rabbis, notes that this is not the 'she was taken' said of Esther (Esther 2:8): the form implies a woman taken against her will, because she was a married woman. The KJV's 'princes' also overstates: these are officials and courtiers, not royal sons.

philological_notes.note: 'They praised'. The same root as 'hallelujah', here used of courtiers flattering a king with a woman's beauty. Rashi says they praised her among themselves, saying 'she is fit for the king'; Ramban allows that they praised her to the king himself.
'She was taken', a passive with no named agent. Radak, citing the rabbis, contrasts it with Esther 2:8 and reads it as 'against her will'.
Officials, court officers, not 'princes' in the sense of a king's sons.

verses.translation_literal: And to Abram he did good on her account, and there was to him sheep and cattle, and male donkeys, and male servants, and female servants, and female donkeys, and camels.
verses.translation_dramatic: And for her sake, Abram was treated well. Sheep came to him, and cattle, donkeys, servants and maidservants, she-donkeys, and camels.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here is the payment, and the text lists it with a flat, accounting tone: seven kinds of wealth, each introduced by 'and'. This is the bride-price, the mohar of the ancient world, paid to the family of a woman a king has taken as wife; Sforno reads it exactly so, as the king's customary payment to the relative who gives her. Since Pharaoh thinks Abram is her brother, he pays the brother. Abram becomes rich by his own lie, and the Hebrew does not comment: it just keeps counting.

The verb heitiv, 'he did good', is the causative of the same root as Abram's wish in verse 13, 'that it may go well for me'. The wish is granted word for word, and the reader should feel how bad the grant is. The KJV's 'entreated Abram well' uses 'entreat' in its old sense of 'treat' and is easily misread today. The KJV also writes 'oxen' for baqar, which is cattle in general; 'he asses' and 'she asses' translate male and female donkeys, and the female donkeys were the prized breeding stock. Camels in the patriarchal stories are debated by scholars as possibly reflecting later periods, when the domesticated camel was common; the text simply lists them.

philological_notes.note: 'He did good'. The causative of yatav, the root of yitav in v. 13. Abram's request is answered with the same word, now as Pharaoh's payment. Ibn Ezra and Radak both link this verse to v. 13.
Female donkeys, valued as breeding stock and mounts. The Hebrew keeps the male (chamorim) and female (atonot) separate.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH struck Pharaoh [with] strikes, great ones, and his house, on the matter of Sarai, wife of Abram.
verses.translation_dramatic: But the LORD struck Pharaoh. Great blows fell on him, and on his house, because of Sarai, Abram's wife.
verses.directors_commentary:
Everything has been done by men until now; now God acts, for the first time in this episode, and the verb is blunt: vayenagga', 'he struck', followed by the noun from the same root, nega'im, 'blows'. The KJV's 'plagued' is not wrong, but it hides the root and the sound play, and the sense of a physical touch. The same root names the skin 'afflictions' of Leviticus 13, and it returns in Exodus 11:1, where God says he will bring one more nega' on Pharaoh before the exodus. Abram does not pray, argue or even speak here. He is silent while God defends the woman he gave away.

Note also the title the narrator gives at last: Sarai is 'wife of Abram', the identity everyone else has forgotten. The phrase al devar, 'on the matter of', is also 'at the word of' (Rashi, citing Genesis Rabbah, imagines her telling the angel 'strike!'), but the plain reading is 'because of the affair of Sarai'. The Hebrew does not say what the plagues were; Rashi reads a disease making intercourse painful, a medieval reading from midrash, not in the text. Radak reads 'his house' as the courtiers who had praised her.

philological_notes.note: 'He struck', a verb from the root 'touch'; the noun nega'im 'blows' follows directly, a cognate accusative: 'struck with strikes'. The root later labels skin disease in Leviticus and the final stroke in Exodus 11:1.
'On the matter of', 'because of'. Rashi also hears 'at the word of', with Sarai speaking and the angel striking. Ibn Ezra takes it simply as 'on account of'.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh called to Abram, and he said, "What [is] this you have done to me? Why did you not tell me that your wife she [is]?"
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Pharaoh summoned Abram. The king of Egypt, still shaken by the blows that had fallen on his house, spoke, and his voice carried through the hall: "What is this you have done to me? Why did you never tell me she was your wife?"
verses.directors_commentary:
Play Pharaoh not as a tyrant but as a wounded, baffled man. The plagues of verse 17 have just told him he has taken a married woman, and he now summons the one who let him do it. Notice the reversal of the scene: the foreigner who holds power over Abram's life speaks as the aggrieved party, and Abram, the chosen one, says nothing. In the ancient Near East a ruler's taking of a woman into his house was a legal act with consequences; taking another man's wife was adultery, a sin against the husband and, to a king, against the gods. Pharaoh's two questions are the language of a wronged party, not of a conqueror.

The opening question, מַה־זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לִּי, is a fixed formula of reproach. It is God's question to the woman in Genesis 3:13 (in the feminine form) and the sailors' question to Jonah in Jonah 1:10, where, as here, a pagan rebukes a man of God for hiding what he knew. The irony is sharp: in the mouth of the pagan king the words are a moral accusation that Abram cannot answer. The KJV's "What is this that thou hast done unto me?" keeps the sense but pads it with "that" and archaic "thou hast"; BBE's "What have you done to me?" loses the demonstrative "this", which carries the exclamation ("what is this!"). The second question, "why did you not tell me", uses הִגַּדְתָּ, a verb of formal declaration, as if Abram owed the king a statement. Hebrew ends on the emphatic pair "your wife, she" (אִשְׁתְּךָ הִוא), which KJV smooths to "she was thy wife", past tense that the Hebrew does not have. The Ramban notes the midrashic view that Pharaoh was struck in his body and so suspected the truth (Ramban on Genesis 12:18, citing Bereshit Rabbah 41:2); Sforno stresses that Abram should not have suspected even a king who upholds the law (Sforno on Genesis 12:18).

philological_notes.note: A formula of reproach: 'what is this you have done?', with the demonstrative zot giving it the force of an outcry. The same words begin God's question in Gen 3:13 and the sailors' in Jonah 1:10. The 'to me' (li) marks the speaker as the injured party.

Hiphil of the root 'to be in front, to make manifest': to declare, announce. It suggests a duty to inform, not casual speech. Ibn Ezra files it among verbs whose first radical nun drops out (Ibn Ezra on Genesis 12:18).

verses.translation_literal: Why did you say, My sister she [is], and I took her to me for a wife? And now, behold, your wife: take [her] and go.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Why did you say, She is my sister, so that I took her as my wife? And now, here is your wife. Take her, and go."
verses.directors_commentary:
Pharaoh's second question is sharper than the first, and its grammar is where the KJV goes wrong. The Hebrew says wa'eqqach, 'and I took her', a plain narrative past: she was taken. The KJV writes 'so I might have taken her', turning an act into a possibility, and in doing so quietly harmonizes with Genesis 20, where Abimelech is told he never touched Sarah. Ibn Ezra and Radak argue that the plagues kept Pharaoh from her, and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan even adds the words 'and I did not come near her'; that is their reading, and our verse itself says only that she was taken 'for a wife'. The phrase 'for a wife' matters too: Pharaoh insists he intended marriage, not a casual taking; Radak and Sforno both read it that way.

Then comes the brusque ending: hinneh ishtekha, 'Here, your wife', as if returning a borrowed object, and two bare imperatives, kach valekh, 'take and go'. The KJV adds 'thy way', which the Hebrew lacks. Rashi contrasts this with Abimelech, who said 'my land is before you'; Pharaoh says 'go, do not stay'.

philological_notes.note: 'And I took'. A narrative past, not a 'might have taken' as in KJV. Compare vatukkach 'she was taken' in v. 15, now with Pharaoh as the speaking subject. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan argue that the plagues prevented any contact.
Two bare imperatives, 'take and go', with no 'thy way'. Radak: take her and go and do not stay in the city.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh commanded concerning him men, and they sent away him and his wife and all that [belonged] to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Pharaoh gave orders about him to his men, and they sent him away: Abram, and his wife, and everything that was his.
verses.directors_commentary:
The scene closes on an escort, not a punishment. Pharaoh commands men concerning Abram, and the verb vayeshalleChu, 'they sent away', is the same word that Exodus will use, in the same stem, for 'let my people go'. The echo is plain: Israel's ancestor leaves Egypt with the wealth of Egypt after the plagues, as his descendants will. That is my own reading of the parallel, not a claim of the text.

Rashi reads the order as a guard and an escort (the Targum has 'they accompanied him'), and Ibn Ezra reads it as an honorable accompaniment; Radak sees an order that no one touch Abram, his wife or his goods, and that they see him out to the border. The KJV's 'his men' adds 'his', which the Hebrew lacks: just 'men'. The last words, 'all that was his', include the gifts of verse 16. Abram is not stripped of the profit from his lie.

philological_notes.note: 'They sent away', in the intensive stem, which can mean to escort or to dismiss. Rashi gives the Targum's 'they accompanied'; Ibn Ezra takes it as an honorable escort, comparing Genesis 18:16.
'He commanded concerning him'. Rashi: 'on his account', to send him off and guard him. Ibn Ezra: a proclamation that no one touch him or his wife. Radak: to guard him and his wife and goods.

events.title: The LORD calls Abram to leave Haran
events.narrative_summary: The LORD tells Abram to leave his land, kindred and father's house for a land he will be shown, and promises to make him a great nation, bless him, and bless all families of the earth through him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word in 12:1–3; the call precedes the departure at age 75 (12:4), so it is placed at Abram's age 75: 75 years from anchor.abraham_birth, margin 1 year (an age covers the whole year). Whether the call came in Ur or Haran is not stated here (cf. Acts 7:2–4) and does not change the date at this precision.

events.title: Abram leaves Haran for Canaan with Sarai and Lot
events.narrative_summary: Abram, seventy-five, takes Sarai, Lot, their goods and people from Haran, enters Canaan and passes through the land to Shechem.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Age 75 at leaving Haran (12:4), same year as the call; offset 1 month after the call for packing, margin 1 month, REGNAL_YEAR. Duration from `urim travel haran canaan shechem --mode donkey`: ~786 km by road at about 32 km/day, ≈ 24 days. A caravan with flocks and people would be slower; the margin of a month covers some of that.
events.ancient_year_marker: When he departed out of Haran, seventy-five years old

events.title: The LORD appears to Abram at Shechem and promises the land
events.narrative_summary: At Shechem the LORD appears to Abram and promises this land to his offspring; Abram builds an altar there.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows arrival at Shechem (12:6), so it starts at the END of the journey. No delay stated; margin 3 days. Duration of the appearance and altar building ~2 hours is an estimate; the tier stays REGNAL_YEAR as the text gives no finer indication.

events.title: Abram pitches his tent east of Bethel and builds an altar
events.narrative_summary: Abram moves to the hill country east of Bethel, pitches his tent between Bethel and Ai, builds an altar and calls on the LORD's name.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Shechem to Bethel: `urim travel shechem bethel --mode donkey` gives ~41 km, 10 h moving, ≈ 1 day, so offset 1 day. The length of his stay is not stated; a month, margin a month, is an estimate.

events.title: Abram travels on toward the Negeb
events.narrative_summary: Abram continues journeying by stages toward the south, the Negeb.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when the Bethel stay ends. Bethel–Negeb is about 84 km straight (~105 km by road); at about 32 km/day that is ~4 days. 'Going and journeying' implies stages, possibly with pauses; margin 2 months.

events.title: Famine drives Abram down to Egypt
events.narrative_summary: A severe famine strikes the land, and Abram goes down to Egypt to live there as a sojourner.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No time word; follows the southward journey. `urim travel bethel negeb egypt --mode donkey` gives ~555 km, ≈ 17 days in all; subtracting the ~4 days of the first leg, ~14 days remain. Margin 1 month for the unstated onset of the famine.

events.title: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister
events.narrative_summary: As they near Egypt, Abram tells Sarai she is beautiful, fears the Egyptians will kill him to take her, and asks her to say she is his sister.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'When he drew near to enter Egypt' (12:11): near the end of the descent, so anchored on the descent's START with offset 13 days of its 14. Margin 2 days.

events.title: Pharaoh's officials take Sarai into his house
events.narrative_summary: When Abram enters Egypt the Egyptians see Sarai's beauty; Pharaoh's officials praise her to Pharaoh and she is taken into his house.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'When Abram came into Egypt' (12:14): starts when the descent ends. Courtiers see her and report, so a few days (3), margin a week.

events.title: Pharaoh gives Abram flocks, servants and camels
events.narrative_summary: For Sarai's sake Pharaoh treats Abram well, and Abram acquires sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants and camels.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Given on account of Sarai (12:16), so right after she is taken; a day, margin a week. Verse 16 is a summary and its gifts may extend until the departure.

events.title: The LORD strikes Pharaoh's house with plagues
events.narrative_summary: The LORD strikes Pharaoh and his household with great plagues because of Sarai, Abram's wife.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No duration is given. Placed one week after Sarai is taken, lasting about two weeks; margin 1 month. Pseudo-Jonathan 12:19 says the plague struck at once; the text only requires that it precede 12:18.

events.title: Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends him away
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh summons Abram, asks why he hid that Sarai was his wife, returns her and has his men escort Abram, Sarai and all they own out.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: After the plagues (12:17–18); the summons and expulsion are one continuous scene, about a day, margin a week.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Abram leaves Haran because the LORD told him to go (12:4).
The LORD's promise to curse whoever treats Abram with contempt (12:3) is echoed in the plagues on Pharaoh's house (12:17).
The land the LORD said he would show Abram (12:1) is shown and promised at Shechem (12:7).
The plagues lead Pharaoh to confront Abram and send him away (12:18–20).
Pharaoh treats Abram well for Sarai's sake (12:16).
The LORD plagues Pharaoh because of Sarai (12:17).
Abram's request that Sarai pose as his sister (12:13) leaves her open to being taken into Pharaoh's house (12:15).

entities.etymology_meaning: The people of Canaan; the name's origin is uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: The inhabitants who were then in the land when Abram arrived at Shechem.

entities.etymology_meaning: The people of Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt.
entities.summary_bio: The people Abram fears will kill him for his beautiful wife; they see Sarai on his arrival.
Men Pharaoh commands to escort Abram, Sarai and all their possessions away.
Court officials who see Sarai, praise her to Pharaoh and have her taken into his house.
A town east of Bethel, marking the eastern side of Abram's camp.
A town in the central hill country. Abram pitches his tent on the hill to its east and builds an altar there.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably related to Akkadian harranu, 'road, caravan route'; uncertain.
entities.summary_bio: A city in northern Mesopotamia where Abram's family had settled and from which he sets out for Canaan at the age of seventy-five.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'teacher' or 'oracle-giver', suggesting a sacred tree where guidance was sought.
entities.summary_bio: The great tree at Shechem, the point to which Abram travels through the land of Canaan.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'dry, parched land', which came to mean 'south'.
entities.summary_bio: The semi-arid southern region of Canaan toward which Abram journeys before the famine.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'the (divine) father is exalted'; the longer form Abraham is given a folk etymology in Gen 17:5.
entities.summary_bio: Son of Terah, who leaves Haran at seventy-five at the LORD's command. He receives the promise of land, descendants and blessing, and travels through Canaan building altars. Famine drives him to Egypt, where he passes Sarai off as his sister.
Abram's nephew, the son of his brother Haran, who goes with him from Haran to Canaan.

entities.etymology_meaning: From Egyptian per-aa, 'great house', the royal palace, later a title for the king.
entities.summary_bio: The unnamed king of Egypt in Abram's day. He takes Sarai into his house and rewards Abram, then is struck by plagues and sends the couple away with all they have.
Abram's wife, very beautiful, who accompanies him from Haran. In Egypt she is asked to call herself his sister and is taken into Pharaoh's house, until the LORD's plagues secure her release.

components.label_value: Living in the land of Canaan
components.evidence_explanation: 12:5–6: he comes to the land of Canaan and passes through it as far as Shechem.
12:10: he goes down to Egypt to sojourn there; 12:20 he is sent away.
12:7: 'To your offspring I will give this land.'
12:16: Pharaoh gives him sheep, cattle, donkeys, servants and camels.
12:4–5: Lot goes with Abram and is taken with him.
12:17: the LORD struck Pharaoh and his house with great plagues.
12:15: the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house; 12:19–20 she is given back.
12:13: Abram asks her to say she is his sister; 12:19 Pharaoh reveals he was told so.

systems.name: Building an altar
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Altars of earth or unhewn stone marked places of encounter with a deity and claimed sacred ground in a land.
rules_and_mechanics: Built at the place of an encounter or arrival.
Dedicated to a named deity.
May be followed by invocation of the god's name.

systems.name: Divine call with promise
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A deity commanding a person to leave home with a promise of land and progeny has parallels in royal and patriarchal narratives; here the call is to a private clan head and not a king.
rules_and_mechanics: The deity speaks first and names the destination only as 'the land I will show you'.
Command is paired with promises of descendants, blessing and a great name.
Obedience is shown by action, as in 12:4.

systems.name: Plague sent by the LORD
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Plagues and disease were understood as divine punishment for wrongs, especially against those under a god's protection.
rules_and_mechanics: The LORD strikes (nagaʿ) a ruler and his house.
The cause is stated in the text.
The affliction ends the wrong done.

systems.name: Calling on the name of the LORD
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Calling on a deity by name was the central act of worship and prayer at a sanctuary, often connected with sacrifice.
rules_and_mechanics: Performed at an altar.
Uses the divine name Yahweh.
Marks public acknowledgement of the deity.

systems.name: Taking a woman into the king's house
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Kings' officials could select attractive women for the palace, which was a step toward marriage into the royal household.
rules_and_mechanics: Officials report to the king.
The woman is taken to the palace.
Her family may receive a bride-price in gifts.

systems.name: Appearance of the LORD
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Deities are said to appear to chosen individuals, often at sacred sites such as great trees, without the vision being described.
rules_and_mechanics: The LORD 'appears' (nirʾah), and the text gives speech but no form.
An appearance is followed by a promise.
The recipient answers with worship.

systems.name: Wife passed off as sister
systems.ancient_near_east_context: A foreigner without protection (a ger) was vulnerable; a husband might be killed to take his wife, whereas a sister could be sought in marriage and negotiated for.
rules_and_mechanics: The wife claims a sibling relationship to protect the husband.
A brother could negotiate a marriage and receive gifts.
The ruse is exposed by divine intervention.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram builds an altar east of Bethel.
system_instances.significance_note: Marks a second sacred site; Bethel later matters for Jacob.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram builds an altar to the LORD who appeared to him.
system_instances.significance_note: Claims the land as a site of worship.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD appears to Abram at Shechem.
system_instances.significance_note: The first reported appearance to Abram, which moves him to worship.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD tells Abram to leave country, kin and father's house for a land to be shown, and promises him a great nation and blessing.
system_instances.significance_note: The start of the patriarchal story and the root of the promise to all families of the earth.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram calls on the name of the LORD at the altar.
system_instances.significance_note: Shows Abram's worship of the LORD as a settled practice.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD promises Abram's offspring the land of Canaan.
system_instances.significance_note: Gives the destination of the call a concrete content, while the Canaanites are still in the land.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD strikes Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai.
system_instances.significance_note: Shows the LORD protecting Sarai and the promise despite Abram's deceit.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Pharaoh's officials see Sarai and praise her to him; she is taken into his house, and Pharaoh himself takes her as a wife (12:19).
system_instances.significance_note: Realizes Abram's fear and sets up the LORD's intervention.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister so that he may live.
system_instances.significance_note: Puts the promise at risk by trading Sarai for his safety.

edges.description: Abram asks Sarai to say she is his sister so that it may go well with him.
Pharaoh's officials commend Sarai's beauty to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh treats Abram well for Sarai's sake and gives him livestock and servants.
Pharaoh has his men send Abram, his wife and all he has away.
Pharaoh asks Abram what he has done and why he did not say Sarai was his wife.
The LORD promises to bless Abram and make his name great.
The LORD tells Abram to go from his country to the land he will show him.
The LORD plagues Pharaoh and his house because of Sarai.
The LORD promises Abram's offspring the land of Canaan.
